concepts.name: HDI: Definition, Purpose, and Conceptual Foundation
key_dimensions: Distinction between economic growth and human development — HDI as a critique of GDP-centric measurement
Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen's foundational philosophy: capabilities approach vs. welfare approach
HDI as a summary measure vs. a comprehensive measure — what it deliberately excludes (inequality, poverty, security)
UPSC trap: HDI measures average achievements, NOT distribution of development

concepts.name: Three Core Dimensions of HDI: Long Life, Knowledge, and Decent Standard of Living
key_dimensions: Exact mapping: Health dimension → Life Expectancy at Birth; Education dimension → two sub-indicators; Income dimension → GNI per capita
UPSC trap: It is GNI per capita (PPP, USD), NOT GDP per capita — significance of this distinction
Why these three and not others: normative choice reflecting minimum capabilities for a dignified life
Each dimension is equally weighted at 1/3 in the final geometric mean — trap: earlier arithmetic mean is no longer used

concepts.name: Life Expectancy at Birth: Health Dimension of HDI
key_dimensions: Goalposts: minimum 20 years, maximum 85 years — used for normalization
What life expectancy captures and what it misses: quality of life, morbidity, disability
UPSC trap: It is life expectancy AT BIRTH, not healthy life expectancy (HALE) — HALE is used in other indices like GHI
India-specific: India's life expectancy vs. global average and implications for HDI rank

concepts.name: Education Dimension: Mean Years of Schooling (MYS) and Expected Years of Schooling (EYS)
key_dimensions: MYS: average years of education received by people aged 25+; EYS: total years a child of school-entry age can expect to receive
Weighting: MYS and EYS are equally weighted within the education sub-index (arithmetic mean of their indices)
UPSC trap: Earlier HDI used Adult Literacy Rate + Gross Enrollment Ratio — this was changed in 2010 revision; current indicators are MYS and EYS
Goalposts for MYS: 0–15 years; for EYS: 0–18 years — normalization using these fixed goalposts

concepts.name: Income Dimension: GNI per Capita (PPP) and its Logarithmic Transformation
key_dimensions: Why GNI over GDP: GNI captures income of residents regardless of location; more reflective of citizens' actual living standard
Why logarithm of GNI is used: diminishing returns to income — doubling income does not double human development
Goalposts: minimum $100, maximum $75,000 (PPP, 2017 constant USD) — UPSC trap: these change across editions
UPSC trap: earlier HDI used GDP per capita; the shift to GNI per capita (PPP) happened in the 2010 revision

concepts.name: Geometric Mean Aggregation: The 2010 Methodological Revision
key_dimensions: Pre-2010: arithmetic mean of three dimension indices — allowed perfect substitutability between dimensions
Post-2010: geometric mean — imperfect substitutability; a low score in one dimension cannot be fully compensated by another
UPSC trap: geometric mean penalizes uneven development — a country with balanced scores ranks higher than one with extreme variation even if averages are equal
Mathematical implication: HDI = (Health Index × Education Index × Income Index)^(1/3)

concepts.name: HDI Classification: Very High, High, Medium, and Low Human Development
key_dimensions: Current thresholds: Very High ≥ 0.800; High 0.700–0.799; Medium 0.550–0.699; Low < 0.550
UPSC trap: India consistently falls in 'Medium Human Development' category — not 'Low'; common confusion
India's rank vs. score: rank fluctuates more than score due to other countries' improvements
Significance for policy: classification affects eligibility for certain international financing and development assistance

concepts.name: Inequality-Adjusted HDI (IHDI): Concept and Divergence from HDI
key_dimensions: IHDI discounts HDI for inequality within each dimension using the Atkinson inequality measure
The 'loss' due to inequality: difference between HDI and IHDI expressed as percentage — India's loss is significant
UPSC trap: IHDI is NOT a separate index but an adjustment to HDI; introduced in 2010 alongside HDI revision
Key insight: countries with similar HDI can have very different IHDI — inequality matters beyond average achievement

concepts.name: Gender Development Index (GDI): HDI Disaggregated by Sex
key_dimensions: GDI = Ratio of female HDI to male HDI — measures gender gaps in human development dimensions
Five groups based on GDI value: Group 1 (high equality) to Group 5 (low equality)
UPSC trap: GDI is NOT the same as Gender Inequality Index (GII) — GDI uses HDI components; GII uses different indicators (maternal mortality, adolescent birth rate, parliamentary seats, etc.)
India's GDI group and what it implies about female vs. male HDI scores across health, education, and income

concepts.name: Gender Inequality Index (GII): Components and Contrast with GDI and HDR Indices
key_dimensions: Three dimensions: Reproductive Health (MMR + adolescent birth rate), Empowerment (parliamentary seats + secondary education), Labour Market (LFPR)
UPSC trap: GII measures LOSS due to gender inequality — higher GII = more inequality = worse outcome; GDI ratio: higher = better
GII replaced the Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) and Gender-related Development Index (old GDI) in 2010
India-specific: India's GII rank is significantly worse than its HDI rank — reproductive health indicators are the major drag

concepts.name: Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI): Relationship with HDI
key_dimensions: MPI dimensions: Health (nutrition, child mortality), Education (years of schooling, school attendance), Living Standards (6 indicators: cooking fuel, sanitation, water, electricity, housing, assets)
UPSC trap: MPI is published in Human Development Report but is NOT a component of HDI; it is a separate complementary measure
MPI vs. income poverty: MPI captures simultaneous deprivations; a person may be above income poverty line but multidimensionally poor
Global MPI (UNDP + OPHI) vs. National MPI (NITI Aayog for India) — India developed its own national MPI with different indicators

concepts.name: Human Development Report (HDR): Publishing Body, Frequency, and Independence
key_dimensions: Published annually by UNDP's Human Development Report Office (HDRO) — UPSC trap: NOT directly by UNDP headquarters, but by a semi-independent HDRO
First HDR published in 1990 — the inaugural report introduced the HDI concept
Each HDR has a thematic focus beyond ranking (e.g., climate change and human development, inequality, etc.)
UPSC trap: HDR is an INDEPENDENT report — the views expressed do not necessarily represent UNDP or UN official positions

concepts.name: Planetary Pressures-Adjusted HDI (PHDI): The Sustainability Dimension
key_dimensions: Introduced in HDR 2020 — adjusts HDI downward based on a country's CO2 emissions per capita and material footprint per capita
UPSC trap: PHDI penalizes high-income countries disproportionately — some 'Very High HDI' countries drop significantly when planetary pressure is factored in
Reflects the tension between human development and environmental sustainability
India's PHDI vs. HDI: relatively small gap because India's per capita emissions and material footprint are low — a rare positive for India

concepts.name: Normalization Formula in HDI: Goalposts and Dimension Index Calculation
key_dimensions: Formula: Dimension Index = (Actual value − Minimum value) / (Maximum value − Minimum value)
Goalposts are fixed across countries and years to allow cross-country and inter-temporal comparisons — UPSC trap: goalposts are periodically revised, causing historical rank revisions
Income dimension uses log of actual GNI and log of goalposts in the formula — unique treatment
Why minimum goalposts are non-zero: to account for subsistence minimum — e.g., $100 for income, 20 years for life expectancy

concepts.name: HDI Rank vs. HDI Score: Why They Diverge and What They Mean
key_dimensions: A country's score can improve while its rank falls — if other countries improve faster
UPSC trap: India's HDI value has improved consistently over decades, but rank stagnation is due to faster improvement by peer nations
Small score differences can cause large rank jumps near threshold boundaries (e.g., around 0.700 or 0.800)
Policy implication: rank is a relative measure; score is an absolute measure — both matter but for different purposes

concepts.name: Critique of HDI: What It Measures and What It Misses
key_dimensions: Does not capture: inequality (addressed by IHDI), gender gaps (GDI/GII), poverty (MPI), political freedom, sustainability (PHDI), happiness/subjective well-being
UPSC trap: HDI has a 'human development paradox' — some oil-rich countries have high income but low education/health scores, pulling HDI down from what GDP would suggest
Data limitation: relies on internationally comparable but often delayed census/survey data — timeliness issue
The index is a useful simplification but not a prescription — it guides attention rather than dictating policy

concepts.name: India's Performance on HDI: Trends, Peer Comparison, and Dimension-wise Analysis
key_dimensions: India in Medium Human Development group; rank around 130s (out of ~193 countries) in recent reports
Dimension-wise weakness: income dimension (low GNI per capita) and education (especially MYS) are the binding constraints vs. health dimension
UPSC trap: India ranks higher on health dimension index than on income or education dimension index within HDI components
Comparison with BRICS peers: India ranks below China, Brazil, Russia but above some sub-Saharan African nations — important for Prelims factual questions

concepts.name: Historical Evolution of HDI Methodology: 1990, 2010, and Post-2010 Changes
key_dimensions: 1990 original: three indicators (life expectancy, adult literacy rate, real GDP per capita PPP), arithmetic mean aggregation
2010 revision: replaced adult literacy + GER with MYS + EYS; replaced GDP with GNI; changed arithmetic to geometric mean; introduced IHDI, GII, MPI
Post-2010 additions: PHDI (2020), updates to goalposts periodically
UPSC trap: questions often mix old and new methodology — e.g., 'which of the following is a component of HDI' — adult literacy rate was, but is NO LONGER

concepts.name: HDI and its Relationship with Other UNDP/UN Indices in the HDR Ecosystem
key_dimensions: HDR ecosystem: HDI, IHDI, GDI, GII, MPI, PHDI — all published together but each measures a distinct concept
UPSC trap: Human Poverty Index (HPI-1 for developing, HPI-2 for developed countries) was the precursor to MPI — replaced in 2010; do not confuse with MPI
Each index addresses a criticism of HDI: IHDI → inequality; GDI/GII → gender; MPI → multidimensional poverty; PHDI → sustainability
Overlap trap: Gender Development Index (GDI) vs. Gender Inequality Index (GII) — both in HDR but measure entirely different things with different methodologies

concepts.name: PPP (Purchasing Power Parity) in HDI Income Dimension: Concept and Significance
key_dimensions: PPP adjustment allows cross-country comparison by accounting for price level differences — $1 buys more in India than in the USA
GNI per capita at PPP (2017 international dollars) is the current standard — UPSC trap: the base year for PPP changes (was 2011 USD, revised to 2017 USD), causing rank revisions
Without PPP, income-based rankings would be distorted in favor of high-price countries and against low-price developing nations
PPP data source: World Bank International Comparison Program (ICP) — not the IMF or UNDP directly
